messages.content:
You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Comprehensive Analysis of SK Hynix ADR Listing: 2.5% Quota, 5-10% Premium, and Index Fund Flow

TEXT:
To prevent disconnection, you are welcome to follow the backup account, where daily content updates will also be available.
SK Hynix is listing ADRs on Nasdaq. The short-term impact is mainly on trading channels and capital structure: an initial quota of 2.5% restricts supply, U.S. equity investors, ETFs, and options ecosystems increase premium elasticity, and will also amplify price volatility in the initial period after listing. Earnings judgement still returns to HBM deliveries, DRAM prices and capital expenditure discipline.
1. This IPO Mainly Changes the Trading Access Point
SK Hynix plans to list its ADRs on Nasdaq this time, to be traded under the symbol SKHY. The timetable provided in the materials is clear: roadshow from July 6 (UTC+8), pricing expected July 9 (UTC+8), trading expected to start July 10 (UTC+8), settlement around July 14 (UTC+8), and new common shares listed on the Korea Exchange around July 29 (UTC+8).
This is more of a trading structure event than a simple exchange listing change. SK Hynix already has London GDRs and Korean domestic common shares; this time, it adds a US ADR channel. The problem it solves is clear: some US institutions cannot conveniently buy Korean local shares or do not want to deal with KRW, time zones, Korean brokers, or local settlement. With the ADR listing, this group can trade SK Hynix with USD during US market hours.
The most important number here is 2.5%. If the ADR were simply another fully convertible trading line, its price would be unlikely to deviate much from the Korean common stock for long; but the underlying shares corresponding to the initial ADR represent only about 2.5% of the total shares outstanding, so the tradable float in the US market is initially small. If US capital is concentrated to buy in, the price will not only reflect the company fundamentals but also whether the US channel has enough supply.
2. 5–10% Premium Originates from Quota, Time Zone and Tools Ecosystem
The market will pay close attention to the prediction that SK Hynix ADR may have a 5–10% premium over Korean local common stock. This is based on market microstructure rather than any upward revisions in earnings forecasts.
First, ADR supply is limited. The initial ADR quota is about 2.5% of total equity and is highly likely to be fully utilized at listing. If thereafter investors wish to convert Korean common shares to ADRs, this is restricted by quota, depository mechanism, and local regulations, and can't simply be regarded as “as long as there are common shares, ADRs can be freely issued.” The harder the supply side, the more easily US market demand can push up the price.
Second, US-side demand is more concentrated. Many global tech funds, semiconductor ETFs, quant funds, and options traders are accustomed to trading in the US market. SK Hynix has long been one of the clearest HBM beneficiaries in the AI storage chain, but trading has mainly been on the Korean market. The ADR listing incorporates this stock into the US trading system, lowering the cost of holding positions, hedging, and portfolio management.
Third, there will be more trading tools. The materials mention that 2x long and 2x short leveraged ETFs based on SK Hynix ADR are expected to be launched around July 13 (UTC+8). If options also get listed smoothly, going long, short, hedging, and volatility trades will become easier. The more trading tools, the more active short-term trading can be, which will also magnify daily fund flows.
This is why MS estimates that the ADR line could account for 10–20% of SK Hynix's total (local and ADR) turnover in the coming months. This proportion is not exaggerated. In Korea local trading, foreign capital already contributes around 29.7%. If some of the US funds shift to ADRs, a 10–20% trading share is realistic.
3. The Conversion Mechanism Determines Whether the Premium Is Sustainable
Whether the ADR premium holds depends on the smoothness of conversion. The judgment in the materials is: converting ADR back to Korean common stock is relatively smooth, but converting Korean common stock to ADR is constrained by the 2.5% quota. This structure will slow arbitrage.
Normally, if the ADR is priced too high, arbitrage funds can buy Korean common stock, convert it to ADRs, and then sell the ADRs, pushing the price gap back down. But the difficulty here is that there is a clear quota on converting common shares to ADRs. Once the initial quota is full, issuing new ADRs requires existing ADR holders to cancel their ADRs and convert them back to local common stock, thereby freeing up quota. This changes arbitrage from a “mechanical brick-moving” process to one of “is there quota available.”
